SOURCE: "Model evaluation for extreme risks", Toby Shevlane, Sebastian Farquhar, Ben Garfinkel, Mary Phuong, Jess Whittlestone, Jade Leung, Daniel Kokotajlo, and 14 others (last author Allan Dafoe). Preprint: no venue is printed, only "arXiv:2305.15324v2 [cs.AI] 22 Sep 2023", with a header date of 25 May 2023. First-author affiliation as printed: "1Google DeepMind". Other affiliations printed: Centre for the Governance of AI, Centre for Long-Term Resilience, OpenAI, University of Toronto, University of Oxford, Collective Intelligence Project, University of Cambridge, Anthropic, Université de Montréal, Mila, Alignment Research Center.

COVERAGE: 20 of 20 pages, 58,240 of 58,240 chars. Body pp. 1-15 and the appendix (p. 20, Table 3) were read in full; references (pp. 16-19) were skimmed for origins.

EMPIRICAL RESULTS: None. This is a position and framework paper with no experiments, datasets or results tables. Its only number is a cited survey figure, and Figure 2 is labelled "purely illustrative".

CLAIMS
- claim: Extreme-risk evaluations fall into two categories: capability and propensity.
  number: none
  setup: definitional; general-purpose frontier models; risks from misuse and misalignment only
  quote: "(a) whether a model has certain dangerous capabilities, and (b) whether it has the propensity to harmfully apply its capabilities (alignment)."
  where: p. 2 (restated p. 3)
- claim: Table 1 names nine dangerous capabilities, described as non-exhaustive: cyber-offense, deception, persuasion and manipulation, political strategy, weapons acquisition, long-horizon planning, AI development, situational awareness, self-proliferation.
  number: none
  setup: generically useful capabilities such as browsing are deliberately omitted; combinations are said to be the riskiest
  quote: "We provide a non-exhaustive list of dangerous capabilities in Table 1."
  where: pp. 4-5
- claim: Alignment evaluations should check five behaviours: pursuing long-term goals other than those supplied, power-seeking, resisting shutdown, collusion with other AI systems, and resisting malicious users' attempts to access dangerous capabilities.
  number: none
  setup: list drawn from prior literature
  quote: "Alignment evaluations should look for behaviours identified in the literature"
  where: p. 4
- claim: A model whose capability profile would suffice for extreme harm should be treated as highly dangerous.
  number: none
  setup: offered as a heuristic, not a tested threshold
  quote: "a model should be treated as highly dangerous if it has a capability profile that would be sufficient for extreme harm, assuming misuse and/or misalignment."
  where: p. 4
- claim: Evaluation results feed risk assessments that inform or bind four kinds of decision.
  number: none
  setup: described as "an ambitious blueprint", not current practice
  where: pp. 2, 6-10
  quote: "The evaluation results feed into processes for risk assessment (Khlaaf et al., 2022), which inform (or bind) important decisions around model training, deployment, and security."
  - Training: delay or pause a run, study the issue, adjust methods, or train a smaller model. Fixes "should target the fundamental issue rather than inducing superficial changes to how the model scores on the available evaluations" (p. 7).
  - Deployment: decide whether to deploy and with which guardrails; staged rollout; continued evaluation after deployment; re-evaluation after model updates; internal deployments are included (pp. 7-9). Table 3 (p. 20) lists the adjustable variables: scale, use restrictions, generality, autonomy, tool use, depth of model access, oversight and moderation, global planning, adjustments to model.
  - Transparency: incident reporting, sharing pre-deployment risk assessments, scientific reporting, educational demonstrations (p. 9).
  - Security: red teaming, monitoring, isolation, rapid response, system integrity (pp. 9-10).
- claim: Three sources of evaluation feed the process: internal evaluation, external research access (likely via API), and external model audit.
  number: none
  setup: the authors concede the external auditor ecosystem "is currently under-developed"
  quote: "There is no substitute for internal model evaluation, given that internal researchers have high context on the model's design and deeper model access than can be achieved via an API."
  where: p. 6
- claim: Table 2 lists design criteria for evaluations: comprehensive (threat models, automated and human-assisted, behavioural and mechanistic, fault-finding, robust to deception, surfacing latent capabilities, model lifecycle, model-level and system-level), interpretable (legible, wide difficulty spectrum) and safe to implement.
  number: none
  setup: aspirational
  quote: "Researchers will need to bring latent capabilities to the surface (for example, by prompt engineering or fine-tuning)."
  where: p. 11
- claim: A narrow alignment pass says little about behaviour under real opportunity.
  number: none
  setup: argued, with the example of a language agent asserting it does not object to shutdown
  quote: "without providing evidence that the model would exhibit desirable behaviour when presented with genuine (or more convincing) opportunities"
  where: p. 10
- claim: Many AI researchers consider extreme risk plausible.
  number: 36%
  setup: a 2022 survey of AI researchers, cited from Michael et al., 2022; the reference title calls it an NLP community metasurvey
  quote: "In a 2022 survey of AI researchers, 36% of respondents thought that AI systems could plausibly "cause a catastrophe this century that is at least as bad as an all-out nuclear war" (Michael et al., 2022)."
  where: p. 3

LIMITS

Stated limitations (section 5.1, pp. 12-13). The text says "at least five" but numbers six:
1. Factors beyond the AI system, such as future tool models and societal resilience.
2. Unknown threat models: "It is difficult to anticipate all the different plausible pathways to extreme risk."
3. Difficult-to-identify properties:
   - Capability overhang: "Models sometimes have capabilities that the AI research community does not realise", with the example of chain-of-thought prompting arriving months after GPT-3.
   - Deceptive alignment: "A situationally aware model could deliberately exhibit desired behaviour during evaluation (Ngo et al., 2022). (This is one reason not to rely solely on behavioural evaluations.)"
4. Emergence: capabilities that appear only at scale, or with U-shaped scaling, undermine forecasting from smaller models.
5. Immature external evaluation and audit ecosystem.
6. Overtrust: "There is a risk that too much faith is placed in evaluation results, leading to risky models being deployed under a false sense of security."

The paper's summary of these: "Model evaluation is a necessary but not sufficient strategy" (p. 13); "not a panacea: it will not catch all extreme risks" (p. 15).

Stated hazards (section 5.2, pp. 13-14):
1. Advancing or proliferating dangerous capabilities through results, evaluation datasets ("dual use because other actors could fine-tune their models on these datasets"), elicitation techniques, and intentionally trained dangerous models (compared to gain-of-function research).
2. Competitive pressure from sharing results between developers.
3. Superficial safety: "if researchers directly train models to pass these evaluations, the evaluations can no longer act as an indicator of risk". This can happen by accidental leakage into pretraining data or intentionally (Volkswagen analogy). The suggested remedy is private held-out evaluations. Even merely not training models that fail exerts selection pressure toward "training methods that produce deceptively aligned models".
4. Harms while running the evaluations: the ARC and TaskRabbit example, crowdworker distress, and "a poorly managed test for whether a model has self-proliferating capabilities could end in actual proliferation".

Unstated limits:
- It offers no thresholds, metrics, validated evaluations or evidence that any evaluation predicts harm.
- It leaves structural risks and incompetence risks out of scope (p. 4).
- It does not use the term "elicitation gap"; the nearest wording is "capability overhang" and "surfacing latent capabilities".
- It is dated: it describes the 2023 landscape (GPT-4, ARC Evals, the draft EU AI Act) and predates most published dangerous-capability evaluation suites and frontier safety policies.

BUILDS ON
- Ngo et al., 2022 (misalignment, situational awareness, deceptive alignment)
- ARC Evals, 2023 and OpenAI, 2023a (GPT-4 system card; self-proliferation and red-team evaluations)
- Perez et al., 2022a,b (model-written evaluations)
- Ganguli et al., 2022 and Wei et al., 2022b (emergence)
- Wei et al., 2022c (chain-of-thought)
- Shevlane, 2022b (structured access)
- Raji et al., 2020, Raji et al., 2022b and Mökander et al., 2023 (auditing)
- Brundage et al., 2018, 2020, 2022
- Liang et al., 2022 (HELM)
- Whittlestone and Clark, 2021
- Khlaaf et al., 2022
- Carlsmith, 2022

CODE: none.

FIGURES: One candidate, Figure 4, p. 6: "A workflow for training and deploying a model, embedding extreme risk model evaluation results into key safety and governance processes." It shows in one diagram how internal evaluation, external access and audit feed the training and deployment risk assessments and reporting. I read only the caption and surrounding text, not the image itself.

PROBLEMS
- `scripts/papers/figures.py captions` returned no output for this PDF; captions were taken from the pypdf text instead.
- Extraction has minor faults: dropped spaces around italic or bold words (e.g. "whymodel", "candiscover") and a few run-together lines. Quotes above have spaces restored where the fault was obvious, so re-check exact spacing before pasting.
- No embedded instructions were found.
- The paper's own inconsistency of "five limitations" against six listed is noted under LIMITS.
